charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 1: Key levers to reduce GHG emissions from Current Policy Scenario (CPS) to Net Zero Scenario (NZS) by 2070E
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: The waterfall chart shows demand-side efficiency and clean-power electrification together accounting for ~60% of the required GHG reduction from CPS to NZS by 2070, with residual emissions (22%) to be handled by CCS and offsets; this underscores that power-sector decarbonisation and industrial efficiency are the highest-priority levers for capital allocation.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 2: Final energy demand projections, Calendar year-ends, 2020-70E (Mtoe)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: India's total final energy demand is set to nearly double by 2050 under CPS but the NZS trajectory holds 2070 demand broadly flat versus 2050 CPS, driven by deep efficiency gains; the divergence highlights the scale of investment required in efficiency and clean technology across industry, transport and buildings.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 3: Energy intensity of GDP, Calendar year-ends, 2020-70E (MJ/Rs.)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: India's energy intensity of GDP is projected to fall by ~86% from 2025 to 2070 under the NZS — a structural demand moderation that reduces the growth in absolute energy needed even as the economy expands, making efficiency-technology companies key long-term beneficiaries.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 5: Projection of residual emissions in Net Zero in 2070E (%)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Cement alone accounts for 40% of India's projected residual emissions under NZS, followed by agriculture (21%) and steel (6%), indicating that CCUS deployment in heavy-industry will be a necessary but technically challenging investment theme through 2070.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 6: Electricity's share of final energy demand under CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2020-70E (%)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Electricity's share of final energy demand nearly triples to 60% by 2070 under NZS versus 22% today, a structural mega-trend that is unambiguously positive for power generators, T&D infrastructure providers and EV-ecosystem players.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 7: Projected electricity consumption under CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2020-70E (TWh)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Total electricity consumption rises roughly 10x from 1,248 TWh in 2020 to ~15,000 TWh under NZS by 2070, with industry and transport electrification dominating the incremental demand — a powerful long-duration tailwind for grid infrastructure and renewable capacity addition.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 8: Projected electricity capacity mix in CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2020-70E (GW)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Non-fossil capacity rises to 98% of India's total installed base under NZS by 2070 versus ~23% in 2020, with solar and wind leading the build-out; nuclear capacity also scales materially, reinforcing the investment case for both renewable developers and nuclear technology suppliers.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 9: Projected electricity generation mix in CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2020-70E (TWh)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Renewables account for over 85% of generation under the NZS by 2070, with storage playing a growing role in firming supply; the remaining fossil generation is almost entirely captive or backed by CCS, validating the structural decline in merchant thermal power.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 11: Estimated cumulative investment requirements for net zero until 2070E (US$ tn)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Total NZS cumulative investment of US$22.7 tn is required by 2070, with the power sector alone absorbing US$12.3 tn (54%), confirming electricity infrastructure as the single largest capital deployment opportunity in India's decarbonisation pathway.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 12: Technology wise split of cumulative total investment required until 2070 (US$ tn)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: T&D and utility-scale renewables (including offshore wind) dominate the cumulative capex requirement to 2070, while GH2 and CCUS/DAC remain relatively small in absolute terms; investors should overweight grid and RE developers for the largest addressable opportunity.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 13: Technology wise split of cumulative total investment required until 2050E (US$ tn)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Through 2050 the investment profile is dominated by electrification and grid, with transport receiving a sizeable share reflecting EV infrastructure; the 2050 vs 2070 comparison shows that green hydrogen and storage investments back-load towards the 2050-70 window as technologies mature.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 15: Projected total net-zero funding needs, availability and gap, Calendar year-ends, 2026E and 2070E (US$ tn)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: A US$6.5 bn financing gap already exists in the 2026-2050 window and widens to US$6.5 tn by 2070, signalling that domestic capital formation and concessional international finance (green bonds, blended finance) will be critical enablers — a watch-point for sovereign ESG risk.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 16: Projected sources and end use of net zero financing supply from 2026 to 2070 (US$ bn)
charts.analyst_caption:
Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
Notes:
(a) 42% share of international finance is calculated by dividing the financing gap (US$4.1 tn) and the expected capital available from international sources in 2026-70 (US$3.1 tn) by the total capital requirement (US$22.7 tn).
charts.commentary: The Sankey-style flow diagram shows banks and NBFCs as the dominant domestic intermediaries (contributing US$1.2 tn) while equity markets and FDI must supply US$4 tn+ of international capital; this points to an essential role for Indian capital markets deepening and green bond issuance to close the financing gap.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 17: Projected primary energy supply under CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2020-70E (Mtoe)
charts.analyst_caption:
Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
Notes:
(a) Non-fossil fuel sources include nuclear, renewable energy and bioenergy.
charts.commentary: Non-fossil sources rise to 86% of primary energy supply under NZS by 2070 versus 13% in 2025, with fossil fuels retained primarily as industrial feedstocks; this trajectory is a structural headwind for conventional coal/oil producers and a tailwind for domestic renewable energy developers and nuclear fuel-cycle companies.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 18: Projected coal demand under CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2020-70E (mn tons)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Coal demand collapses from 1,256 mn tons in 2025 to just 161 mn tons by 2070 under NZS — an 87% decline — confirming structural demand destruction for thermal coal companies and underscoring the urgency of portfolio repositioning for coal-heavy conglomerates.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 19: Projected oil demand under CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2020-70E (mn tons)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Oil demand peaks around 2050 at 402 mn tons under CPS but falls sharply to 149 mn tons under NZS by 2070, primarily driven by transport electrification and efficiency; this divergence frames the long-term stranded-asset risk for oil refiners and marketing companies if transition is accelerated.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 20: Projected natural gas demand under CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2020-70E (Billion Metric Standard Cubic Meter (BMSCM))
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Natural gas demand rises under both CPS and NZS through 2050 before falling back to 92 BMSCM by 2070 under NZS — staying above today's level — indicating that gas infrastructure (CGD networks, pipelines) retains medium-term investment relevance as a transition fuel, particularly for sectors hard to electrify.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 22: Projected green hydrogen demand for various end-use sectors under CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2050 and 2070E (mn tons)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Green hydrogen demand rises from near-zero today to 50 mn tons by 2070 under NZS, with steel, refinery, fertiliser, and shipping as the dominant end-uses; this confirms green hydrogen is a late-cycle (post-2040) opportunity with the largest near-term demand pull from industrial decarbonisation, not transport.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 23: Projected SAF demand under CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2050E and 2070E (bn liters)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Sustainable Aviation Fuel demand rises to 32 bn litres by 2070 under NZS, roughly 4x the CPS level, highlighting biofuel refiners and feedstock suppliers as emerging clean-aviation beneficiaries as India's aviation sector grows.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 24: Projected ethanol demand under CPS and NZS, Calendar year-ends, 2050E and 2070E (bn liters)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Ethanol demand stays broadly flat at 20-22 bn litres across CPS and NZS scenarios through 2070, suggesting that blending mandates provide a floor for sugar/distillery companies but offer limited upside from the energy transition itself relative to hydrogen or SAF.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 26: Projected share of scrap in steel in steel under NZS, Calendar year ends, 2020-70E (%)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Steel scrap usage rises to 40% of production by 2070 under NZS from 22% today, structurally favouring EAF (Electric Arc Furnace) steelmakers and scrap aggregators while pressuring BOF-based integrated steel players with high coal dependence.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 27: Projected share of scrap in aluminium under NZS, Calendar year ends, 2020-70E (%)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Secondary (scrap-based) aluminium grows to 40% of production by 2070 under NZS versus 27% today, reducing the carbon-intensity of aluminium smelting; aluminium recyclers and those with captive scrap access are well-positioned relative to primary smelters reliant on coal-fired power.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 28: Projected clinker to cement ratio under NZS, Calendar year ends, 2020-70E (x)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: The clinker-to-cement ratio declines from 0.67x in 2020 to 0.55x by 2070 under NZS as blended cement adoption deepens, which structurally lowers carbon intensity but is achievable with existing technology — a positive for cement companies already investing in blended product mix.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 29: Cumulative CETM recoveries from e-waste between 2025 and 2047 in baseline scenario (%)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: E-waste recovery rates for copper, nickel, graphite and neodymium rise steeply from near-zero in 2025 to 60-80% by 2047 in the baseline scenario, while lithium and cobalt recovery lags at 20-40%; this highlights a critical dependency on organised e-waste recycling infrastructure that remains largely absent in India today.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 30: Demand for copper at different time horizons across CPE and NZE scenarios, Calendar year-ends, 2025-70E (mn tons)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: India's copper demand rises 22x from 1.4 mn tons in 2025 to 43.6 mn tons by 2070 under NZE, reflecting electrification of transport, grid and renewable installations; this creates a very long-duration positive thesis for copper processors and recyclers listed in India.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 31: Demand for graphite at different time horizons across CPE and NZE scenarios, Calendar year-ends, 2025-70E (mn tons)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Graphite demand surges from 0.7 mn tons in 2025 to 30.8 mn tons under NZE by 2070, almost entirely battery-driven; India currently has no significant natural graphite mining, making import diversification and synthetic graphite production a strategic bottleneck in the EV battery supply chain.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 32: India's CETM demand as share of global demand in the Net Zero Scenario, Calendar year-end, 2050 (%)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: India's share of global CETM (Critical Energy Transition Minerals) demand reaches 9% for copper and cobalt, and up to 14% for lithium by 2050 under NZS — material enough to affect global pricing dynamics and justify domestic mineral security policies as a key ESG policy risk for battery-related industries.

charts.report_title: ESG - India @ 2070, The great energy rewrite for Net Zero
charts.chart_title: Exhibit 34: Projected electricity consumption in data centers, Calendar year-ends, 2030-70E (GW)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: NITI Aayog, Kotak Institutional Equities
charts.commentary: Data center electricity demand is projected to leap from 3 GW in 2030 to 80 GW by 2070, making it one of the fastest-growing new load segments for India's grid; this supports the investment case for dedicated renewable PPAs, grid-scale storage developers, and RE-powered data center operators.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: India's merchandise exports grew by 13.8% YoY in Apr 2026
charts.analyst_caption: Source: Ministry of Commerce (MoC); CEIC; CLSA
charts.commentary: India's total merchandise exports accelerated to 13.8% YoY in April 2026, the second-highest monthly level on record, driven by a surge in non-oil non-GnJ exports; the broad-based pickup across categories signals improving external demand traction beyond commodity volatility.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: ...with non-oil non-GnJ exports growing at above 10% YoY
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: Data for Apr for all years.
charts.commentary: Stripping out gold and oil, India's core export momentum has stayed above 10% YoY — a structural positive suggesting domestic manufacturing competitiveness is rising and the export recovery is not purely a commodity-price story.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: Fuel exports remained quite strong in Apr 2026
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: G&J = Gold, silver and precious stones. Data for Apr for all years.
charts.commentary: Fuel exports held up strongly while engineering goods and electronics also contributed positively in April 2026; textiles remained a laggard, reinforcing the need for sector-specific policy support to revive labour-intensive export industries.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: Exports to ASEAN* countries more than doubled in Apr 2026...
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: *Includes details for Malaysia, Singapore and Vietnam only. *GCC countries only include UAE and Saudi Arabia.
charts.commentary: Exports to ASEAN nations more than doubled YoY in April 2026, while GCC and South Asian destinations also grew sharply — consistent with India rerouting trade flows away from conflict-affected Middle East lanes and deepening ties with Southeast Asian partners.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: ...but to GCC* has fallen very sharply and the share has halved
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: *Includes details for Malaysia, Singapore and Vietnam only. *GCC countries only include UAE and Saudi Arabia.
charts.commentary: GCC's share of India's exports has halved, a direct casualty of the India-Pakistan war's disruption of Middle East trade routes; this structural diversion risk to Gulf destinations is a key watch item for sectors such as gems & jewellery and engineering goods that rely heavily on that corridor.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Quantifying impact of high oil prices
charts.chart_title: India's CAD has been very well behaved in the post-pandemic period
charts.analyst_caption: Source: RBI, CSO, CLSA. Note: 4QFY26 are CL estimates
charts.commentary: India's current account deficit averaged a remarkably low 0.8% of GDP over FY20-FY26, well below the 3.1% average of FY14-FY19; this improved structural starting point means an oil-driven CAD deterioration to 2-2.5% of GDP, while uncomfortable, would still be within historically manageable territory.

charts.report_title: India Rates & FX - Fortnightly rates and FX view
charts.chart_title: Government cash balance (Rs tn)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: RBI, CEIC, Kotak Mahindra Bank estimates
charts.commentary: Government cash balances have declined sharply from around Rs4 tn to approximately Rs1 tn recently, with a projected recovery to ~Rs4 tn by end-May as RBI dividend and GST collections flow in. This seasonal drawdown-and-refill pattern means banking system liquidity should tighten temporarily before rebounding, keeping overnight rates anchored within the LAF corridor.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: India's merchandise imports grew 10.0% YoY in Apr 2026...
charts.commentary: Import growth of 10% YoY in April 2026 was broad-based across oil and non-oil categories, reflecting resilient domestic demand; the moderate pace relative to export growth is supportive of a narrowing trade deficit, though the war's commodity-price pass-through remains a key risk.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: ...thus growing 8.6% YoY in 11MFY26
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: Data for Apr for all years.
charts.commentary: On an 11-month cumulative basis imports grew 8.6% YoY in FY26, a pace that — combined with the export acceleration — is gradually improving India's external balance, though the full impact of commodity disruptions from the conflict is still working through.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: Valuables decline in share vs imports, along with electronic goods
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: G&J = Gold, silver and precious stones. Data for Apr for all years.
charts.commentary: The share of gold & jewellery and electronic goods in imports declined in April 2026 while commodities held firm; this compositional shift could ease pressure on the current account if sustained, though it partly reflects demand softness rather than genuine substitution.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: Imports from LatAm* countries grew sharply...
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: *Details of other LatAm countries were unavailable. *GCC countries only include UAE and Saudi Arabia.
charts.commentary: Imports from Latin America (Brazil/Peru) surged sharply, likely reflecting India diversifying commodity sourcing away from conflict-affected GCC and Middle East routes; this supply-chain pivot raises near-term logistics costs but reduces geopolitical concentration risk.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: ...and the share of GCC* countries came off sharply
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: *Details of other LatAm countries were unavailable. *GCC countries only include UAE and Saudi Arabia.
charts.commentary: GCC's share of India's import sourcing dropped sharply, a direct signal of war-related supply disruption from the Gulf; with GCC being the primary crude and fertiliser corridor, any prolonged dislocation would structurally lift India's energy import bill and complicate the current account outlook.

charts.report_title: India Rates & FX - Fortnightly rates and FX view
charts.chart_title: Average 30Yr x 10Y sovereign spreads (bps)
charts.commentary: Global 30Yr-10Yr sovereign spreads have widened sharply in May, with France at 254 bps and Japan at 160 bps leading the move, versus the US at 46 bps and UK at 54 bps. The steepening reflects global fiscal concerns and long-end supply pressure that are also influencing Indian bond yields, with the old 10Y GS 2036 trading at 7.08% and Kotak expecting a range of 7.05-7.25%.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: India's merchandise deficit was at US/US$28.4bn in Apr 2026...
charts.commentary: The monthly merchandise trade deficit widened to US$28.4bn in April 2026, elevated versus the FY26 average, underscoring that while exports are recovering the import bill — particularly commodities — remains sticky and limits near-term current account improvement.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: ...which is estimated to be the highest in 13 years
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: Data for Apr for all years. Assuming US$5 nominal GDP growth of (1.5)/(3.8)% YoY in 4QFY26/FY27.
charts.commentary: At an estimated 1.21% of GDP, the April 2026 trade deficit as a share of GDP is the highest in 13 years — a significant deterioration that, if sustained, would pressure the rupee, widen the current account deficit, and constrain RBI's easing room.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: India's G&S exports grew faster than imports in Apr 2026...
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: *Government's estimates for services trade for Apr 2026. Data for Apr for all years.
charts.commentary: Goods and services exports combined grew faster than imports in April 2026 on a YoY basis, with services maintaining its structural surplus role; the services engine (primarily IT/BPO) continues to partially offset the merchandise trade deficit and supports the overall balance of payments.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Full impact of the war yet to come
charts.chart_title: ...and the G&S trade deficit narrowed marginally versus Apr 2025
charts.analyst_caption: Source: MoC; CEIC; CLSA. Note: *Government's estimates for services trade for Apr 2026. Data for Apr for all years. Assuming US$5 nominal GDP growth of (1.5)/(3.8)% YoY in 4QFY26/FY27.
charts.commentary: The combined goods-and-services trade deficit narrowed marginally year-on-year in April 2026 as services surplus (IT exports, travel) offset goods weakness; however the deficit at ~0.2% of GDP remains a watch item given the war's potential to widen the merchandise gap further in coming months.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Quantifying impact of high oil prices
charts.chart_title: Crude oil prices play an important role in determining India's CAD
charts.analyst_caption: Source: RBI, CSO, CLSA. Note: 4QFY26 are CL estimates
charts.commentary: The tight co-movement between India's current account balance and crude oil prices illustrates the direct transmission channel — every US$10/bbl rise adds roughly 0.5% of GDP to the CAD, making the trade deficit the primary macro vulnerability in a high-oil environment.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Quantifying impact of high oil prices
charts.chart_title: Foreign capital flows could remain lower than CAD in FY27
charts.analyst_caption: Source: RBI, CSO, CLSA. Note: 4QFY26 are CL estimates
charts.commentary: India's net foreign capital inflows (FDI + FPI + ECB + other) are projected to fall short of the widening CAD in FY27 under an oil shock scenario, implying a deterioration in the BOP balance and putting pressure on the RBI to run down FX reserves or allow INR depreciation.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Quantifying impact of high oil prices
charts.chart_title: Rupee has a close relationship with the BOP balance (or FX reserves withdrawal/accumulation)
charts.commentary: Historical data confirm that sharp BOP deficits — especially when accompanied by a large CAD — have consistently been associated with episodes of INR weakness; CLSA warns the rupee could average Rs94-95/US$ in FY27 if crude stays at US$100/bbl, with a peak around Rs97/US$.

charts.report_title: India Rates & FX - Fortnightly rates and FX view
charts.chart_title: Comparison between Indian crude basket and brent futures (US$/bbl)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: PPAC, Bloomberg, Kotak Economics Research
charts.commentary: The Indian crude basket has tracked Brent futures closely and has fallen toward the low end of recent ranges, with both benchmarks hovering in the upper-$60s/bbl range as of mid-May 2026. Lower crude reduces India's import bill and BOP pressure, providing a mild tailwind for the INR and moderating headline inflation.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Quantifying impact of high oil prices
charts.chart_title: …and it has a close relationship with global crude oil prices
charts.commentary: India's headline WPI has tracked global crude oil prices with a high degree of correlation, with the WPI surge in FY22-FY23 closely mirroring the Brent spike; at US$100/bbl crude, CLSA projects WPI could rise to 8.25% YoY in FY27, posing secondary pass-through risks to CPI via industrial input costs.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Quantifying impact of high oil prices
charts.chart_title: …due to which CPI inflation could stay under 5%
charts.commentary: CLSA's CPI scenario analysis shows that even under a US$100/bbl crude assumption and a 5-6% retail fuel price hike, CPI inflation could be kept below 5% in FY27 if the government manages pass-through — a key argument for why the RBI may not be compelled to hike rates, preserving monetary policy space.

charts.report_title: India Rates & FX - Fortnightly rates and FX view
charts.chart_title: FX reserves (US$ bn)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: CEIC, Bloomberg, Kotak Economics Research
charts.commentary: India's FX reserves have pulled back from a peak of ~$705 bn to ~$697 bn in recent weeks, reflecting RBI dollar sales to defend the INR. The reserves buffer remains comfortable at over $690 bn, providing the RBI adequate firepower to limit INR depreciation without exhausting its war chest.

charts.report_title: India Rates & FX - Fortnightly rates and FX view
charts.chart_title: Trend in 40-currency real effective exchange rate index (2015-16=100)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: CEIC, Bloomberg, Kotak Economics Research
charts.commentary: India's 40-currency REER has trended broadly sideways-to-higher since 2021 while USDINR has risen from ~73 to ~84+, indicating that nominal INR weakness has been largely offset by India's relatively higher inflation versus trading partners. The REER remaining elevated implies limited competitiveness gain from INR depreciation, but also that real appreciation pressure is contained.

charts.report_title: India Rates & FX - Fortnightly rates and FX view
charts.chart_title: RBI's net forward position (US$ bn)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: CEIC, Bloomberg, Kotak Economics Research
charts.commentary: RBI's net forward position has swung sharply negative (net short dollars) over the past two years, reaching around -$80 bn in the greater-than-1-year bucket. This unwinding of the forward book adds to spot dollar supply but also signals that the RBI's intervention capacity in the spot market is being increasingly supplemented by forward sales.

charts.report_title: India Rates & FX - Fortnightly rates and FX view
charts.chart_title: Trends in RBI FX intervention (US$ bn)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: CEIC, Bloomberg, Kotak Economics Research
charts.commentary: RBI net spot and forward dollar purchases have turned positive again in recent months after a sustained period of net selling, suggesting the central bank is rebuilding reserves opportunistically. This tactical shift implies the RBI is comfortable letting USDINR find a new, slightly higher equilibrium rather than defending a specific level aggressively.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Quantifying impact of high oil prices
charts.chart_title: We expect better nominal and weaker real growth in FY27
charts.commentary: At US$100/bbl crude, nominal GDP growth could rise to 12% YoY in FY27 as higher inflation inflates the numerator, while real GDP growth is squeezed to around 5.7% — the divergence between nominal and real growth is a key risk for corporate earnings quality, as revenue growth may look healthy in nominal terms while volume and margin metrics weaken.

charts.report_title: India Rates & FX - Fortnightly rates and FX view
charts.chart_title: Trend in trade balance and capital flows (US$ bn)
charts.analyst_caption: Source: CEIC, CDSL, Kotak Economics Research
charts.commentary: India's goods trade deficit has been persistently negative at -$15 to -$20 bn per month, while services surplus provides a partial offset; net FPI flows have been volatile and recently turned negative. charts.report_title: India Economics - Quantifying impact of high oil prices
charts.chart_title: Domestic crude oil production at lowest level in 21st century…
charts.commentary: India's domestic crude production has fallen to its lowest level of the 21st century at around 27,500 thousand tonnes in FY26, down from peaks above 38,000 thousand tonnes a decade ago — this structural decline in domestic supply is a key driver of the rising import dependency that makes the macro more sensitive to global oil price shocks.

charts.report_title: India Economics - Quantifying impact of high oil prices
charts.chart_title: …and, thus, import dependency has risen to c.89%
charts.commentary: India's crude oil import dependency has risen to approximately 89% of total consumption in FY26, up from around 81% a decade ago — this near-total reliance on imports means any global oil price shock translates almost fully into a higher import bill, amplifying the CAD and BOP risks quantified elsewhere in this report.

charts.commentary: India's ethanol blending rate jumped to 18-20% by Nov-25 from low single digits in 2014, showing rapid policy-driven scale-up; sustaining this trajectory to E25 by 2030 requires further near-doubling of ethanol supply, pointing to continued volume tailwinds for sugar/grain ethanol producers.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 1: Southern Oscillation Index
charts.analyst_caption: Source: Bloomberg and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: The Southern Oscillation Index has recently turned negative, signalling an El Nino-favourable atmospheric pattern; the shift into negative territory from the La Nina highs of 2020-22 implies drier monsoon conditions for India in 2026, which is the foundational risk the report addresses.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 2: Monsoons rainfall during El Nino years
charts.analyst_caption: Note: Colour coding denotes strength of El Nino. Red denotes strong, yellow denotes moderate and green denotes weak. The dotted lines denote the sub-normal and deficient rain thresholds. Source: CEC, Reuters, NOAA, IMD and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Rainfall during past El Nino years has varied widely — from near-normal to deeply deficient (as low as -20.8% from LPA in 2002 and -18.4% in 2009) — indicating that El Nino is a necessary but not sufficient condition for a bad monsoon, which underpins Nomura's cautious-but-not-alarmed view.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 3: Southwest monsoon forecast probability by IMD
charts.analyst_caption: Source: IMD and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: IMD's forecast assigns 35% probability to 'deficient' (below 90% LPA) and 31% to 'below normal', meaning roughly two-thirds of probability mass lies in sub-normal territory — a meaningful headwind that markets should price into rural consumption and food-inflation expectations.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 4: Scatter-plot of food production growth vs rainfall deviation
charts.analyst_caption: Note: For monsoons, we calculate the June-September rainfall deviation from 2018 onwards using daily data. For prior years, we rely on annual data from IMD. Source: CEIC, IMD and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: The scatter shows a broadly positive relationship between rainfall and food production growth, but the correlation is loose — sub-normal rains have frequently coexisted with positive food output growth, supporting the thesis that irrigation coverage and improved seeds have reduced rain-dependence.

charts.report_title: Asia FX - HOT Long SGD-IDR, Maintain maximum conviction level
charts.chart_title: Fig. 3: Long SGD/IDR, conviction level 5/5, targeting 14,200 by end-August 2026
charts.commentary: SGD/IDR has trended sharply higher since January, with Nomura progressively raising conviction from 2/5 to the maximum 5/5 and lifting the target to 14,200 by end-August 2026; the annotated entry ladder shows disciplined add-on entries at each conviction step, with the spot already near 14,200 at time of writing.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 5: Scatter-plot of agri yield vs rainfall deviation
charts.analyst_caption: Note: For monsoons, we calculate the June-September rainfall deviation from 2018 onwards using daily data. For prior years, we rely on annual data from IMD. Source: CEIC, IMD and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Agricultural yield shows a similarly weak relationship with rainfall deviation in sub-normal years, echoing the food production scatter; the wide dispersion around the trend line implies structural factors (irrigation, MSP, crop mix) are at least as important as rainfall quantum.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 6: Food production growth vs Rainfall
charts.analyst_caption: Note: Bars in black denotes El Nino years. For monsoons, we calculate the June-September rainfall deviation from 2018 onwards. For prior years, we use annual data sourced from IMD. Source: CEIC, IMD and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Food production (y/y, red line) does not neatly collapse every time rainfall deviates negatively (grey bars), with 2018 and 2023 showing resilient output despite sub-normal rains; this historical pattern is the empirical backbone of Nomura's 'shock absorbers are in place' argument.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 9: Food inflation vs rainfall
charts.analyst_caption: Note: Bar in black denotes El Nino episodes. For monsoons, we calculate the June-September rainfall deviation from 2018 onwards. For prior years, we use annual data sourced from IMD. Source: IMD, and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Food inflation (red line) does not track rainfall deviations (grey bars) in a mechanistic way — several sub-normal rain years produced only modest inflation spikes — underscoring that government MSP policy, buffer stocks, and import decisions are powerful intermediary forces.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 10: Scatter-plot of food inflation vs rainfall deviation
charts.analyst_caption: Source: CEIC and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: The scatter of food inflation against rainfall deviation shows near-zero slope in the sub-normal range, confirming that weaker rains alone do not guarantee higher food prices; policy and global commodity prices dominate the inflation outcome, which supports the RBI keeping rates on hold rather than pre-emptively tightening.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 13: Rice stocks vs buffer norms
charts.analyst_caption: Source: CEIC and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Rice stocks have been consistently above buffer norms since 2020 and remain well above the minimum threshold as of early 2026, providing a substantial food-security cushion that can be deployed via the PDS to contain retail rice inflation even if the Kharif harvest disappoints.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 14: Wheat stocks vs buffer norms
charts.analyst_caption: Source: CEIC and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Wheat stocks have tightened relative to their early-2020 highs but remain above buffer norms, though the narrowing buffer is a watch point; if El Nino weakens the winter Rabi crop too, the wheat stock cushion could erode faster than rice, leaving less policy room in H2 FY27.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 15: Cereals price tracker
charts.analyst_caption: Note: This is Nomura's proprietary price tracker based on daily prices across key markets in India. Shaded regions correspond to periods of deficient rains and El Nino. Nomura's proprietary price tracker based on daily prices across key markets in India. Shaded regions correspond to periods of deficient rains and El Nino. Source: CEIC and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Cereal price inflation has moderated in recent quarters and is currently running at low single digits, suggesting the buffering effect of abundant government stocks is working; a continuation of this trend is key to Nomura's benign headline CPI projection of ~5.0% for FY27.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 16: Pulses and edible oils tracker
charts.analyst_caption: Note: These are Nomura's proprietary price trackers based on daily prices across key markets in India. Shaded regions correspond to periods of deficient rains and El Nino. Source: CEIC and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Pulses and edible oil prices remain the most volatile components, with pulses tracking elevated y/y and edible oil prices rebounding — these two categories pose the primary upside risk to food inflation in a deficient monsoon year and would be the channels through which El Nino most directly hits the CPI.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 17: Farming revenue vs cost growth
charts.analyst_caption: Source: CEIC and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Farming revenue index growth (3m-ma) has recently re-converged with cost index growth after a sharp post-COVID divergence; if El Nino squeezes output, the gap could turn negative for farmers — a key downside risk to rural purchasing power and hence to rural-facing consumer names.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 18: Farming Terms-of-trade
charts.analyst_caption: Source: CEIC and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Farming terms-of-trade (revenue/cost index) have been trending up since 2023, reaching multi-year highs — this improved farm profitability provides a buffer against a single bad monsoon and reduces the probability of a sharp rural demand collapse even if rainfall disappoints.

charts.report_title: India Economics - El Nino may not scorch the economy
charts.chart_title: Fig 19: FMCG volume growth: Rural vs urban
charts.analyst_caption: Note: FY26 is only for Q1-Q3 average. Source: NIQ and Nomura Global Economics
charts.commentary: Rural FMCG volume growth has consistently outpaced urban since FY24 (6.3% vs 3.5% in FY26), a recovery that El Nino could interrupt; two-wheelers and rural FMCG are the most direct equity plays to watch — a deficient monsoon would likely narrow the rural-urban gap and pressure rural-skewed consumer staples.

charts.report_title: India Strategy - A tough summer, austerity measures, the history and the future
charts.chart_title: EXHIBIT 2: While better than the 2012-14 phase, the current situation remains grim and is the second worst this millennium. It is equivalent to that of 2022, when fuel prices were hiked by ~10 rupees in a span of 15 days
charts.commentary: India's months of import cover from foreign-currency assets has fallen to levels comparable to 2022 (the worst post-2014 episode) and well below the comfortable 16+ months seen in 2020-21, signalling meaningful FX vulnerability; a sustained slide below ~9 months would historically trigger sharper policy tightening and fuel-price hikes.

charts.report_title: India Strategy - A tough summer, austerity measures, the history and the future
charts.chart_title: EXHIBIT 3: RBI has large dollar liabilities totalling $78 billion, of which $28.5 billion is due within the next 12 months
charts.commentary: RBI's forward book shows $28.5 bn maturing within 12 months against a backdrop of already-stressed reserves, with the 1-month and 1–3 month buckets dominating near-term maturities and USD sales running hot; this rollover wall reduces the RBI's ability to intervene aggressively to defend the rupee and raises the probability of further pass-through depreciation.

charts.report_title: India Strategy - A tough summer, austerity measures, the history and the future
charts.chart_title: EXHIBIT 5: Many of the top import categories for India are sensitive sectors and cannot be restricted without adverse effects on domestic sectors
charts.analyst_caption: Source: Ministry of Commerce, Bernstein Analysis
charts.commentary: Petroleum Products dominate at $131 bn (nearly 2x the next category), with Precious Metals ($85.9 bn) and Chemicals ($63.3 bn) also large; sectors highlighted in blue (already targeted) cover a small share of the total, while the bulk of imports sit in politically or economically untouchable categories — constraining the government's ability to deliver a material improvement in the trade deficit through import restrictions alone.

charts.report_title: India Strategy - A tough summer, austerity measures, the history and the future
charts.chart_title: EXHIBIT 6: The gold import duty surge has already made the import duties on yellow metal highest in India's post-liberalization history
charts.analyst_caption: Source: Press Reports, PIB, Bernstein Analysis
charts.commentary: Gold import duties have risen to approximately 18% in 2026, the highest since the 'Total Ban Era' pre-1990 and sharply above the 2012-13 peak (~10%) when the current-account crisis last forced aggressive action; this level is likely near the ceiling of what is politically and practically enforceable, meaning further gold-import compression from duty increases is limited.

charts.report_title: India Strategy - A tough summer, austerity measures, the history and the future
charts.chart_title: EXHIBIT 7: The average fuel hike per hike cycle in the last 10 years have been 11%, leaving a lot of room for current hikes
charts.commentary: Historical petrol and diesel retail price hike cycles have averaged ~11% per episode over the past decade, whereas the current cycle has only delivered ~3.2% so far; this gap suggests that if the government follows the historical playbook — as it did more aggressively in 2021 and 2022 — there is meaningful further upside to pump prices, with negative read-through for OMC losses, consumer staples demand, and inflation.

charts.report_title: India Strategy - A tough summer, austerity measures, the history and the future
charts.chart_title: EXHIBIT 8: Assuming the government factors in crude cooling down to $100 a barrel, a further 12-13 rupees of hike might still be required to avoid OMC losses
charts.analyst_caption: Source: PPAC, Bernstein Analysis and Estimates
charts.commentary: At $90/bbl crude the remaining appreciation needed is ~₹1.4/l for petrol and ~₹0.4/l for diesel, but at $110/bbl this jumps to ~₹24/l for petrol and ~₹22.5/l for diesel; OMC profitability is acutely sensitive to the crude trajectory, and unless crude falls materially from current levels, a politically painful double-digit per-litre hike appears unavoidable to restore marketing margins.
